prediction:
THOUGHT: The patient is a late-30s woman who is markedly immunosuppressed (recent kidney transplant, recent treatment for acute cellular rejection, on prednisone and mycophenolate). She presents with painful perianal ulcers and diarrhea. Key diagnostic data point strongly toward CMV: high-level CMV viremia (172,000 copies/mL), histopathology showing enlarged cells with intranuclear “owl’s‑eye” inclusions, and positive CMV immunohistochemical stain; the ulcer-base PCR is reported positive (consistent with CMV). These findings are essentially diagnostic of CMV mucocutaneous disease (CMV proctitis/perianal CMV ulceration). C. difficile is also positive and likely explains the diarrhea but is an unlikely primary cause of the discrete deep perianal ulcers. Other causes of painful perianal ulcers in immunocompromised patients (HSV, VZV, Crohn disease, Behçet, ischemic/aplastic lesions from antiphospholipid thrombosis) remain possible alternatives, but histology and virology make them much less likely here.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Cytomegalovirus (CMV) perianal mucocutaneous ulceration / CMV proctitis (most likely; supported by high CMV PCR, characteristic histology with owl’s‑eye inclusions, and positive CMV immunostain)  
2) Herpes simplex virus (HSV) proctitis/perianal herpes (important alternative in immunocompromised patients but less likely given CMV-confirmatory histology)  
3) CMV disseminated infection with colitis/proctitis (systemic CMV disease accompanying mucocutaneous lesions; closely related to #1 and possible given high-level viremia and thrombocytopenia)  
4) Clostridioides difficile–associated proctocolitis with secondary perianal skin breakdown/ulceration (explains diarrhea and can cause perianal irritation but does not account for CMV histology)  
5) Inflammatory bowel disease (perianal Crohn disease) or Behçet-related aphthous/perianal ulcers (less likely given acute presentation, absence of typical systemic/oral findings, and CMV-proven ulcer pathology)

Case Information:
A woman in her late 30s presented with a 4-day history of perianal pain. Her medical history included systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, and external hemorrhoids. Six months prior, she underwent a deceased donor kidney transplant. One month before presentation, she was hospitalized for acute cellular transplant rejection managed with immunosuppressive therapy. Current medications included prednisone 5 mg daily and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg twice daily. She developed diarrhea 1 day after admission.

Physical Examination:
On admission, she was afebrile and normotensive. Total body skin examination revealed 1- and 3-cm tender, round perianal ulcers with a clean base. Another 4-mm round ulcer was present at the superior intergluteal cleft. There were no ocular or oral ulcers.
